title: In 76,215 human genomes, the X chromosome adds ten times more variant deficit at conserved coding than at conserved non-coding sites, so strong recessive selection acts on few non-coding bases
abstract:
On the X chromosome, which males carry in one copy, conserved protein-coding sites have many fewer variants than on other chromosomes, but conserved non-coding sites have only slightly fewer. This matters because conserved non-coding DNA shows weak selection in human samples, and hidden recessive selection, which rare autosomal variants cannot see but males expose on the X, was a possible reason; the data limit strong recessive selection to a few percent of these bases.

We used gnomAD v4.1 (76,215 genomes) on chrX (132.6 Mb callable) and chr4, 7, 8 and 13 (543 Mb). The deficit is 1 minus observed/expected single-nucleotide variants, with expected counts from neutral bases of the same 3-base context, repeat state and 1-Mb window. Conserved means a 241-mammal phyloP score of 2.27 or more. Conserved missense sites: deficit 0.465 on X and 0.273 on autosomes (extra 0.192, 95% CI 0.167-0.222). Conserved non-coding sites: 0.122 and 0.104 (extra 0.018, 0.011-0.027); with a neutral reference near genes the extra is 0.006 (-0.005 to 0.015), while coding stays near 0.2. The singleton excess is amplified on X by a similar factor for both (1.29 and 1.27). A pre-registered test found non-coding mutations not more recessive than missense. In a population-genetic model of eight statistics, a purely additive model is rejected for conserved non-coding bases; uniform partial dominance (h about 0.2-0.3) and an additive majority with 1-3% strongly recessive bases fit equally well, and a fully recessive subclass with fitness cost of 0.03 or more includes at most 3-7.5% of bases. The model splits the autosomal deficit into a lower mutation rate (0.05-0.06) and selection (0.048), in agreement with a de novo calibration (0.045). Conserved regulatory elements show more X amplification of common-variant loss than additivity allows, a hint of weak recessive selection.

Limits: absolute dominance is not identified (h moves from 0.1 to 1.0 for a 2% difference in X mutation rate); the model does not fit strongly selected coding sites; X and autosomal genes differ in content; four autosomes were used.

display.caption: (a) Variant deficit on the X chromosome against the deficit on four autosomes for conserved bases (phyloP >= 2.27), by class; large symbols pool all conserved bins (95% bootstrap intervals), small points are single phyloP bins; lines are model expectations for dominance h = 0.5, 0.25 and 0.1. (b) Zoom on non-coding classes and synonymous sites, with model lines without (faint) and with (solid) the fitted mutation-rate offset of 0.06. (c) Extra X deficit (X minus autosomes) at conserved and non-conserved bases with 95% bootstrap intervals.

(a) Singleton excess on X divided by singleton excess on autosomes, for conserved bases of each class (95% bootstrap intervals). (b) Dominance h from joint fits of eight statistics under six model variants (fitted or theoretical X population size; shared mutation offset, female mosaic dominance, or allele-frequency statistics only), with 95% profile intervals scaled for model misfit. Missense and stop-gain fits are poor.

(a) Split of the autosomal deficit of conserved non-coding bases into a mutation-rate offset (grey, 95% profile) and a selective deficit (orange) from joint fits, compared with the selective deficit from an independent de novo calibration (green). (b) Largest fraction of conserved non-coding bases that can be fully recessive, by fitness cost of that subclass, with the rest additive or h = 0.3. (c) Largest fraction of non-conserved cCRE bases with fully recessive selection, from singleton shares alone (dashed) or singleton and common-variant shares (solid).
